title: TreeMap and LinkedHashMap
learningObjectives: Store entries by key in TreeMap with keys maintained in sorted order
Preserve predictable insertion order with LinkedHashMap
Explain how natural key ordering or a Comparator affects TreeMap
Use the Map interface while selecting an implementation deliberately
Test key replacement and iteration order in both implementations

understand.concept: TreeMap orders entries by key. LinkedHashMap maintains predictable encounter order, normally insertion order. Both implement Map.
understand.whyItMatters: TreeMap and LinkedHashMap helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Map implementations and their contracts

Map<K,V> associates each key with at most one value. Adding a mapping for an existing key replaces its previous value. The Map interface defines operations such as put, get, containsKey, remove, keySet and entrySet; it does not itself promise a universal iteration order.

## HashMap

HashMap uses hashing for key lookup and makes no iteration-order guarantee. Its typical lookup and insertion performance is constant time when hash codes are distributed well. Never use a printed HashMap order as a stable expected result.

## LinkedHashMap

LinkedHashMap maintains a predictable encounter order, normally insertion order. Replacing the value for an existing key does not create a second key. It is useful for reports or user interfaces where entries should be traversed in the order they were first inserted. It can also be configured for access order, which is useful in cache designs.

## TreeMap

TreeMap stores entries in key-sorted order using the keys' natural ordering or a supplied Comparator. Basic get, put and remove operations take logarithmic time. Keys must be mutually comparable under the selected ordering. A comparator that returns zero treats keys as the same map key, so a later put replaces the existing mapping.

## Choose and test deliberately

Declare a variable as Map<K,V> when code needs only map operations. Select HashMap, LinkedHashMap or TreeMap according to ordering requirements. Test duplicate-key replacement separately from iteration order, and ensure custom key classes implement equals and hashCode consistently when used with hash-based maps.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<Integer,String> values = new java.util.TreeMap<>(); values.put(2,"B"); values.put(1,"A"); System.out.println(values.keySet()); } }
examples.explanation: put creates key-value mappings; get retrieves the value associated with the requested key.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<Integer,String> values = new java.util.LinkedHashMap<>(); values.put(2,"B"); values.put(1,"A"); System.out.println(values.keySet()); } }
examples.explanation: Putting a second value under the same key replaces the first mapping rather than creating a duplicate key.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<String,Integer> values = new java.util.TreeMap<>(); values.put("pear",2); values.put("apple",1); System.out.println(values.keySet()); } }
examples.explanation: getOrDefault returns the supplied fallback only when the key has no mapping; it does not replace the map contents.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<Integer,String> values = new java.util.TreeMap<>(java.util.Comparator.reverseOrder()); values.put(1,"A"); values.put(2,"B"); System.out.println(values.keySet()); } }
examples.explanation: LinkedHashMap iterates in insertion order while TreeMap iterates by sorted key order; the output demonstrates the different contracts.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<String,Integer> values = new java.util.LinkedHashMap<>(); values.put("first",1); values.put("second",2); System.out.println(values.get("second")); } }
examples.explanation: Map is the interface type used by the variable, while the TreeMap instance supplies sorted-key iteration.

practise.guidedTask: Insert keys out of order into TreeMap and LinkedHashMap. Print key sets and explain sorted-key order versus insertion order.
practise.independentTask: Build a word-frequency report using a Map, then present the entries in sorted key order with TreeMap.
hints: A Map has unique keys; inserting an existing key replaces its value.
LinkedHashMap normally preserves insertion order; TreeMap sorts by key; HashMap promises neither order.
TreeMap uses its comparator to distinguish keys, so compare returning zero means the keys occupy the same mapping.
practise.challenge: Use a reverse-order Comparator with TreeMap and test duplicate key replacement; explain why a Map stores only one value per key.
